MR. ARGUE    ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION FROM NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the house and my position in the house. I rise to inform the house that I have severed all my connections with the New Democratic party and, as a consequence, yesterday requested Your Honour to change the location of my seat.
My decision made at Regina to the Assiniboia N.D.P. executive was taken only after much careful and heart searching thought. The most difficult part of this decision was the realization that it meant leaving a group of men who had become very close to me, and who had worked and co-operated with one another for a period of almost four years. I leave eight hard working, sincere members of parliament who have served their country and their constituencies with distinction, and whose devotion to duty is an example to the whole house.
The second great difficulty in the decision I was making was that it was bound to hurt many good people of independent thought who had been my close friends within the C.C.F. These were the people who day after day, often at great sacrifice, went about trying to build a new party based on social justice and economic equality, and with the basis of control in the constituency organization. The consequence to them of my action I profoundly regret. In its justification I can only respond that the integrity of the Canadian nation, in my judgment, required me to make this decision.
I have already stated that in my opinion the N.D.P. was in the control of a small labour clique, and that their hold on the party was sure to continue and strengthen with the affiliation of more union locals. With delegates representing trade union locals and other labour bodies predominating over constituency delegates at conventions, discussion and persuasion on the convention floor becomes superfluous and votes become exercises merely to rubber stamp previously agreed to platform directives. It would be most dangerous to the democratic process to have a party gain power,
the effective control of which resided in a handful of labour leaders situated outside the House of Commons. This was the impelling reason why I have left the N.D.P.
As to the future, I shall merely say that I desire to seek re-election to parliament in my own riding of Assiniboia, and that I expect to make a further announcement bearing on my political future at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for its kind indulgence.

Mr. Speaker, according to the press today Mr. Khrushchev sent a message in that sense to the President of the United States and suggested there should be co-operation of a scientific, technical and material nature between these two nations in outer space.
As the house will recall, this is a matter which I had the honour of bringing before the United Nations in September, 1960. On an earlier occasion I spoke of this to the Canadian Bar Association and put forward the proposition that in view of the tremendous potentialities in outer space for good and evil, action should be taken among the nations before it is too late to achieve the means to ensure to all nations, great or small, sovereign equality in outer space and, as well, to ensure that outer space will be used for scientific and peaceful purposes. It was also suggested on behalf of Canada that international agreement should be reached as soon as possible on the use of outer space entirely for peaceful purposes, regulating against its use for military purposes.
Anything that may be done to advance such an agreement will certainly receive Canada's support. It is one of the most outstanding problems facing mankind. After what happened yesterday and the two previous flights that were made by U.S.S.R. astronauts, it must be generally considered by mankind that now is the time to prevent developments

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night i was dealing with the question of the export of hydro power generated in Canadian plants. I should like to make it quite clear that I am dealing with this subject in a very general way and that my remarks have no relationship to the specific and unique case relating to downstream benefits on the Columbia river. These benefits, Mr. Speaker, are a payment to Canada by power at site in compensation for the flooding of a beautiful valley in British Columbia. This flooding would be of no benefit to British Columbia unless the people of British Columbia received-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but X think our sound amplification system is not working well and I hope hon. members will dispose themselves to listen, because it is almost impossible to hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I say, unless these benefits flow to the people of British Columbia, unless they are of value to the people of British Columbia then there is no excuse for the flooding of this valley. This question, of course, because of its peculiarity and its uniqueness, is the subject of negotiation between the federal government and the government of British Columbia.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that the export of power should, I think, be considered in the


same way as the export of any other commodity such as gas or oil, except that provision must always be made for the orderly recapture of this power as required by Canada. We do not export gas and oil except when there is a surplus to foreseeable Canadian requirements. The same policy should apply to hydro power.
At this session, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has introduced the subject of a national power grid. Eventually this grid will be built and will bring advantages to all parts of Canada. However, this grid must be based upon hydro power because it will bring power from remote localities, where hydro power is usually developed, to large load consuming centres. Thermal power on the other hand, whether it be coal, oil, gas or nuclear power, is generated in plants adjacent to load consuming centres, and thermal power plants can be scaled in proportion to a particular need. As the load grows extra turbines can be added. By comparison, hydro installations usually result in very large blocks of power becoming immediately available. One cannot dam half a river. When a dam is completed and the reservoir is filled, then the power is available but local demand cannot use all this power. It can only use a small proportion of it.
It seems to me that initially much of such power will be available for export and, as I say, if it is controlled under a treaty or regulations established by the national energy board then the surplus power can be sold for a definite period of time and provision can be made for its orderly recapture. Thermal power usually involves high operating costs; hydro power has large capital costs and low operating costs. Now, however, the gap between power costs, comparing hydro with thermal, is closing. The increased cost of money and increase in transmission costs will ultimately increase the cost of hydro power, but if we wait until local demand can use all the hydro power at any particular site then I think we shall be losing a chance to develop a very real national resource.
We in British Columbia have some 33 million horsepower capacity of hydro energy which is undeveloped, and there is no reason why this hydro energy cannot be developed as markets are available and as prices can be secured which will cover the cost of carrying the new installations until such time as either local demand or the provision of a national grid will allow the marketing of this power in Canada.
I have been asked many times what the Conservative government has done for the people of Canada, and when from memory I have given only a partial list, invariably

The Address-Mr. Broome
I am then asked why we do not let the people know what we are doing. Evidently our press relations need improving, because the story of the real achievements of this government has not been fully understood.
When this government took over in June, 1957 we had already entered a recession. The famous hidden report of government economists, presented to the Liberal government in the spring of 1957, warned the government that all was not well with the economy of the country. Unemployment was rising, business was slowing down, exports were falling off, and it was time for strong government action to control these forces of recession. The Liberal government chose to ignore this report. They maintained their tight money policy, claiming that inflation was the real menace, not recession.
Looking back it is easy to understand how this happened. They had been in power during war years, first the second world war and then the Korean war. They then had no problem of unemployment. After the war there was the gigantic job of rebuilding Europe and satisfying the pent up demand for consumer goods. There was no problem in selling either at home or abroad. We could sell all we could produce and within reason at whatever price we wished to ask. It was a market where salesmen did not have to sell, they simply took orders.
By 1957 this easy selling era had disappeared and we were once again meeting aggressive competition in the markets of the world, and increasing foreign competition in our domestic market. Japan and western Europe had rebuilt their war-destroyed industrial power, and with active government assistance were increasing their sales at the expense of ours.
It is a fact of nature, Mr. Speaker, that when any species refuses to evolve to meet changing environmental conditions that threaten its existence, then that species disappears; and this, I suggest, can be applied to governments also. I do not mean to imply that the Liberal party is as dead as the dodo, the mastodon or the dinosaur, but their policy in 1957 was strictly for the dinosaurs.
In 1957 they offered a six bucks raise in the old age pension to stimulate consumer spending when they had a $300 million surplus. They offered nothing for housing, although housing starts had dropped to the lowest point in years and they had $150 million voted by parliament for N.H.A. loans which they would not release. They offered no aid to exporters, nothing to small business, no reduction in taxes, nothing except wartime thinking for a peacetime economy. Today the Liberal party says "Liberals have
the answers", but the same leaders who say this today had none of the answers in 1957. Five years ago they had none of the answers; today they say they have them all. What a change in five years.
When this government took office the $150 million in the N.H.A. fund was immediately released. A few months later the total was increased to $400 million; in May, 1958 to $750 million; in March, 1959 to $1 billion; in March, 1960 to $1.5 billion, and in September, 1961 to $2 billion. Total amount of loans that may be made by approved commercial lenders was increased 50 per cent from $4 billion to $6 billion. Down payments on new homes were lowered to 5 per cent, which is $500 on a $10,000 home.
These bold moves led to unprecedented expansion in the housing industry, an easier road to home ownership for the average Canadian, and the provision of jobs for 1.5 million Canadians in construction and in manufacturing, supplying timber, cement, household appliances and furnishings, and the thousand and one items which go into a home. We have extended the scope of this program to include loans to build university residences, loans to municipalities to build sewage disposal plants and extensions to trunk sewers. The new Vancouver sewage disposal plant could not have been built without this assistance, and there are new residences going up on the campus of U.B.C. which could not have been built without this assistance.
In the field of social justice, payments to old age pensioners were increased to $55, and this month to $65. The same increases were applied to pensions for the blind and disabled, and for those on old age assistance. Residence requirements were lowered from 20 years to 10 years and old age pensions were made portable so they could be paid to those Canadians who live outside Canada for health or other reasons.
It may not be generally known that this government increased from 2 per cent to 3 per cent the proportion of revenue received from federal sales tax and personal and corporation income taxes earmarked to pay for old age pensions. The result was that in 1961 pension payments were $592 million and tax receipts to cover those payments were $603 million, leaving a surplus of $17 million. Under the Liberals the old age pension fund had a cumulative deficit of around $500 million. We are attempting to make this fund self-supporting and therefore payable as of right. Undoubtedly the recent increase will throw the fund into a temporary deficit position, but

The Address-Mr. Broome the growth in our economy will provide increased revenue which will eventually bring the fund back into a balanced position.
In 1962-63 old age pensions amounting to some $737 million will be paid to 930,000 Canadians. This money will be spent for goods and services, and will provide a stimulus to the entire Canadian economy. In total all social justice payments have been increased from $1.3 billion in 1956-57 to $2.3 billion in 1960-61, an increase of 77 per cent.
The speech from the throne indicated the desire of the government to introduce a system of contributory and portable pensions. As reported at page 531 of Hansard the Minister of National Health and Welfare had this to say about this proposal:
The second aspect of making adequate income provision for our senior citizens relates to the question of contributory old age survivors and disability insurance which, as indicated in the speech from the throne, is to be placed before parliament if the provinces view with favour a suitable amendment to section 94(a) of the British North America Act.
The government's objective in this regard is clear cut. Our aim is to have an integrated program of old age income security which, in addition to the universal flat rate benefit, will provide a graduated benefit for all those who can reasonably afford further provision for their old age and who have not already undertaken it under private pension plans or other contractual agreements.
As the house knows, this government, through federal-provincial conferences called by the Minister of Justice, has been endeavouring to reach agreement on the question of having our constitution amended in Canada. This has been our hope. We now feel it is necessary to ask the provinces to agree to an amendment to the B.N.A. Act so we may proceed to carry out our decisions in this regard.
In another area very vital to Canada, what is our record in regard to export trade, because Canada is more dependant upon export trade than any other industrialized nation? At least one job in five depends upon export trade, and in British Columbia the ratio is even higher. Dealing with commodity exports only, the total for 1956 was $4.8 billion. In 1961, taking the latest figures available, October 1960 to October 1961, they were $5.7 billion, an increase of $900 million. In 1956 we had a trade deficit of almost $600 million, while in 1961 we will have a balanced trade with exports slightly greater than imports. Also, Mr. Speaker, as you know our trade will be at an all time record high.
This has not happened by chance, but because this government went out to aid our exporters in every way possible. We eliminated the exchange premium on the Canadian dollar and immediately made our

goods more competitive in world markets. We provided export credit facilities to provide long term financing for capital goods exports, and we made $200 million available for this purpose. To date almost $186 million has been committed, and this session we have increased this fund to $300 million. These facilities allow Canadian manufacturers to sell fully manufactured goods on credit and meet the competition of foreign firms in this regard, particularly United States firms operating through the export-import bank. We are participating in more international trade fairs than ever before; we are sending overseas more trade missions than ever before, and our trade commissioner service has been told to get out and sell Canadian goods.
Any discussion of trade would be incomplete without a reference to the European common market and the strong possibility that Britain will join this association. As far as I am concerned, I believe that what is best for Britain's long range interests will also be best for Canada. I would prefer a strong Britain in the common market to a weak Britain outside. Many people have suggested that Canada should join the common market. The truth of the matter is that we cannot join the common market. As the Minister of Finance said in a speech to the Kiwanis club in Montreal on February 1, when referring to the European economic community:
Six European countries seeking closer integration, partly for economic and partly for political reasons, signed in March, 1957 what has come to be known as the treaty of Home, which provides for the establishment of their common market.
He went on to point out that this treaty applies only to European countries, although there is provision for associate countries to join the common market. These associate countries were originally the French community in Africa and underdeveloped countries whose products would be complementary to and would not conflict with European products. They are countries which are not industrialized. There is no provision for industrialized countries such as Canada to join the European common market and, as the minister went on to say when speaking to high ranking officials in Europe, "We cannot join, and we would not be welcome even if we tried."
Finally, Mr. Speaker, before I leave the subject of trade let me point out that not only is our export trade at a record high but we now have a more diversified trade pattern. We have markedly increased our exports to the United Kingdom, western Europe, South America and commonwealth markets other than the United Kingdom. Although the

United States is still our largest customer, all our eggs are no longer in one basket.
In regard to contributions to the provinces, it is a little known fact that up to March 31, 1961 the cumulative increases in federal contributions to the provinces and provincial institutions exceeded the cumulative budget deficit for the same period of time by almost $300 million. In other words, if these additional payments had not been made there would have been no deficit. For instance, payments to all provinces for hospital insurance this year will be $284 million.
Let us look at the picture as far as payments to British Columbia are concerned. In 1956-57 the Liberals contributed $7 million to the trans-Canada highway construction. This year we will contribute $17 million. By the time this highway is completed the federal government will have contributed over $100 million to the province of British Columbia, or about 25 per cent of all the money paid to all the provinces. An additional $40 million will have been spent on the highways and national parks in British Columbia since 1957. Yet the highway is plastered with signs leading the motorist to believe this is the work of the Social Credit government alone.
In the fiscal year 1956-57 the Liberal government gave just over $17 million in conditional grants to the province of British Columbia. In the present fiscal year this government will contribute over $70 million. Payments for old age security, family allowance, blind and disabled persons allowance, veterans payments, hospital construction grants, unemployment insurance, old age assistance, and so on amounted in 1956-57 to $137 million and in 1960-61 to $245 million, which includes $22J million paid to British Columbia for hospital insurance for 1960-61. Just over $33 million was paid to British Columbia for hospital insurance prior to 1961, and in the 1962 estimates $26.4 million is provided for this same purpose.
Therefore by the end of the 1962 fiscal year British Columbia will have received1 over $82 million for hospital services. In the province of British Columbia we were already paying a 5 per cent sales tax, of which 2 per cent was earmarked for hospital services. When the federal government agreed to cover half of the costs of hospital services the premier of British Columbia indicated that the province was in a deficit position in regard to payments for hospital insurance, and that these payments from the federal government would be used to offset this deficit.
Well, the deficit has been far offset by now; yet there has been no reduction in our sales tax, and the money which is coming from the federal government to help pay the cost of hospital insurance in British Columbia is going into consolidated revenue to be used for
The Address-Mr. Hellyer whatever purposes the provincial government may wish to use it. I wonder how many Vancouver taxpayers know that each year this government has paid back to the provincial government, as a special grant, 50 per cent of the taxes collected from the B.C. Electric Co.
We have doubled the per capita allowance for university students. We have increased grants for hospital construction. We have brought in a ship building subsidy to help our ship building industry-a measure which is of major importance to the west coast. We have increased the capital of the industrial development bank to $400 million and made this money available as loans to small business. We held down freight rates by government subsidy to help, in particular, British Columbia and the maritimes.
All these measures, together with many others which I have not named, were aimed at stimulating the Canadian economy, increasing purchasing power, increasing exports and accelerating the development of our national resources. We were fighting unemployment and a sluggish economy caught in a typical North American recession.

speechtext:
The speech from the throne is more notable for its omissions that for what it contains. It includes only passing reference to the great and important issues of the day. Not much is proposed in order to get Canada going again.
Dynamics of growth such as trade, industry and immigration, for example, are scarcely considered at all. The urgency of deciding on a defence policy for Canada is not realized. This view is shared by many thoughtful observers. For instance, the Globe and Mail of January 20, 1962, in an editorial entitled "The Uncertain Trumpet" had this to say:
There was a general expectation in Canada this week that the speech from the throne opening what presumably is the last session of the present parliament would be a resounding election manifesto. It has proved to be nothing of the kind. It would be difficult to imagine anything further from a blast of trumpets. It is in fact, a curiously thin and inadequate statement from a government which must soon face the voters.
The financial editor of the Montreal Gazette takes a similar attitude in his column. On January 19 he is quoted as saying:
A reluctance to come to grips with really basic issues is also apparent in the references to the British entry into the common market.
He was referring to the speech from the throne. The government's defence policy, or lack of policy, remains unchanged. There is no indication as to whether or not Canadian troops will be armed with atomic warheads.
1104	HOUSE OF
The Address

Mr. Hellyer However, the question is becoming increasingly urgent with the passing of the months since the last session of parliament ended. Since that time, Canada has acquired its first F-101 interceptors. The Royal Canadian Air Force has recently taken over operational control of the Bomarc station at North Bay; we are advised by the minister that it will be in charge of maintenance, heating and so on. Furthermore, an Honest John battalion has been sent to join our brigade group in Europe. In each case a decision has yet to be made as to whether or not these weapons will be armed with nuclear warheads. Two of them, at least, we have been told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) only reached maximum effectiveness when so armed. We were told earlier, too, that there was, as an alternative, the possibility that they could be armed with conventional warheads. We have since learned, and it was really no surprise to us, that no conventional warheads have been designed, let alone are readily available for our armed forces. This is a ludicrous position. We are spending a lot of money for weapons systems which are now operational except for the fact that they are unarmed, and we are continuing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars for further weapons systems which are in the same category.
This lack of decision on the part of the government is extremely frustrating to our allies. I know that the United States government and the armed forces are thoroughly frustrated because they cannot get any decision one way or another from the Canadian government. I know, too, that our allies in Europe feel the same way. If a decision were made not to arm our armed forces with atomic warheads, at least that would be understood and the necessary adjustments would follow. On the other hand, if we should decide to arm them, that decision would be understood and appreciated. But the failure to reach any decision is altogether incomprehensible to our allies in NATO and Canada has become the laughing stock of the world as a result.
Discussing this question of atomic warheads yesterday afternoon, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) put forward his own policy in this respect or, at least, he stated that his policy was different from that held by frontbench members of his party. Closer examination leads one to wonder, however, where it is actually a third policy or whether it is just part of the same old confused policy. He said:
After we have explored every possible avenue for working out a successful agreement we must then accept the advice of our professional military people. If they consider it is necessary to the defence of Canada that we have nuclear weapons. I believe we have no other course to follow. However, I emphasize that this should not be done until every avenue has been fully explored toward


reaching a successful agreement on disarmament. The taking on of nuclear weapons prior to that would hopelessly prejudice any discussions or negotiations that might lead to a successful agreement.
That is quite a mouthful. How long does the hon. member think we should wait before a decision is made? How long does he think disarmament discussions will continue to take place? They have already been going on for years, but no concrete results have been achieved. Does he think we should wait another three years? Does he think we should wait another five? Unless the hon. member is prepared to state categorically the length of time he has in mind, his proposal makes no sense at all; it is in fact no different from the one put forward from time to time by other members of the government party.
Mr. Pallet!: Does the hon. member have an alternative proposal?

speechtext: Yes. I think a decision should be made one way or another.

This is a most urgent matter and it deserves discussion in more detail; I shall perhaps have an opportunity to go into it more deeply in another debate. But at the present time I urge the government who, after all have the responsibility under our system for making a decision, to announce its intentions in this regard.
What about the dynamics of growth. Has the government's immigration policy helped or hindered our national development? On April 5, 1957, at Toronto the Prime Minister promised a vigorous immigration policy to bring immigrants to Canada to increase the population. Later in the same month, on April 25, he indicated to the ethnic press association in Toronto that annual immigration up to 4 per cent of the population was feasible. This worked out to approximately 640,000 persons per annum. That was quite a vision, but the fulfilment has been something of a revelation. Immigration has been declining steadily. Last year saw the lowest number of people entering Canada in a decade.
On the other hand, emigration is increasing. More people are leaving Canada for their native lands and the United States. Most alarming of all is the fact that the people who are leaving Canada are those who have the most skill. We talk about the necessity of greater skill among our working force, yet the people who are leaving us by tens of thousands are those who have the greatest skills. These are the people we most urgently need if our country is to grow and develop.
Why are they leaving in such large numbers? Why does this trend accelerate? How

can it be reversed? I think one of the reasons for its acceleration must be the lack of challenge in this country. It must be the lack of faith these people have in Canada. If it were otherwise they would not leave but would stay and assist as best they can in the development of this nation.
I think the problem was aptly summed up by the late Judith Robinson in one of her columns in referring to the summary fashion in which the cancellation of the Avro Arrow was undertaken by this government when she said the tragedy to her was not the cancellation of a particular project but the loss of faith of a whole generation of young Canadians in the future of their country. This, Mr. Speaker, is in fact the real tragedy, one which has not yet been overcome.
There is little indication that the government has given much thought to the relationship between interest rates and economic growth. This is a subject which merits study. What is the relationship between government deficits and interest rates? At the time of the election in 1957 one of the things we were not promised was deficits. Speaking at a press conference in Saskatoon on May 27, 1957 the Prime Minister included among his promises the following:
John Diefenbaker said today a Progressive Conservative government could carry out its declared policy, reduce unnecessary taxes "and still do it on a balanced budget".

The hon. gentleman claims that taxation was reduced. Total taxation has certainly increased and the deficits we were not promised have been growing in total. The inference of this and other statements made by the Prime Minister at that time was that we would have Diefenbaker, not deficits. Well, Mr. Speaker, we hit the jackpot, we got both.
There are important questions to be answered. Why does the level of unemployment remain so high? Why is the rate of growth of the labour force declining so rapidly? The statistics are interesting. For example, between 1956 and 1957, January to January, the growth in the labour force was 202,000, between 1957 and 1958 it was 195,000; between 1958 and 1959 it was 99,000; between
1959	and 1960 it was 127,000; and between
1960	and 1961 it was 193,000. In January of 1962 the growth stood at only 13,000. There has been a dramatic decline from a growth of between 100,000 and 200,000 per year to an annual growth of only 13,000 people. Where have they gone? What has happened to them? Are they all going back to their native lands or the United States? Are they too discouraged to remain in the labour force? Perhaps some
The Address-Mr. Hellyer of them are remaining at school for a longer period of time. It is to be hoped that is so, but it would be interesting to know.

speechtext:
The hon. member would be in a better position than I to judge that.
One of the most important failures of the speech from the throne was its failure to indicate any positive initiative toward the far reaching re-organization of world trading patterns. There was no evidence of a change of heart on the part of the government. There was no evidence of the emergence of a realistic attitude. There was much evidence of a negative, obstructionist and unyielding attitude at Accra and since.
One does not have to look far for the reports and I wish to mention just two or three. The Ottawa Citizen of September 14 last carried the following news item datelined Accra, Ghana:
Canada has warned Britain that she cannot be the leader of the commonwealth and a member of the European common market, too.
In an emotional intervention at Wednesday's session of the commonwealth economic consultative council, finance minister Donald Fleming said an eloquent requiem for the system of trading preferences that has bound the British nations together for a generation.
On the same day a Canadian Press dispatch was carried in the Ottawa Journal datelined Accra:
Finance minister Donald Fleming of Canada said Wednesday the United Kingdom is irretrievably "launched on a slippery slope" to membership in the European common market. As a result the commonwealth will never be the same again.
Mr. Clark Davey, the Globe and Mail correspondent wrote in that paper on the same date:
Commonwealth members, with Canada's trade minister George Hees making the keynote speech, emphatically told Britain today that she must choose between the European common market and the commonwealth.
In an uncompromising statement to the commonwealth economic conference here, Mr. Hees presented what amounted to a flat Canadian demand that Britain not join the common market.
Canada had expected more, Mr. Speaker. We had hoped for something positive. We hoped our ministers would go there to preserve as best they could the real interests of Canada and the free world. Many were dismayed at the attitude displayed by the representatives of the government at that time. This was well summed up by the Globe and Mail on October 3, 1961 when it stated editorially that Canada had expected more from its representatives at Accra.
The attitude of this government seems to be typical of Tory attitudes throughout the generations. It is not unlike the attitude of

The Address-Mr. Hettyer the late R. B. Bennett in the thirties. It might interest hon. members to know that in the book "Neville Chamberlain" by Iain Macleod, at page 161, there appears an extract from a letter written by Chamberlain to his sister on August 21, 1932, from Ottawa, at the time of the imperial conference. The extract is as follows:
In spite of the anxieties they caused us I have no complaint to make of the Australians or New Zealanders. They had to think of the difficulties of their own people . . . They were quite straightforward about it.
Bennett was a different proposition. He alternately blustered, bullied, sobbed, prevaricated, delayed and obstructed to the very last moment.
I am sure that the same attitude Mr. Chamberlain observed at that time on the part of the Tory government of that day was displayed by our representatives at the Accra conference. Canadians generally favour Canadian participation and British participation in enlarging the trading area. On numerous occasions this has been voiced by many leaders in the industrial and commercial world. I should like to cite just two or three examples. Mr. John Meyer, the Gazette financial editor, is reported as follows:
Uncertainty about Canadian policy towards the European common market was described last night as one of the strongest inhibitions on economic growth.
John Meyer, financial editor of the Gazette, told the Montreal chapter of the national office management association, that a decision in favour of applying for an associate membership in the common market would do more to prolong the present recovery than any other factor.
Another distinguished gentleman is reported as follows:
Moncton, N.B.-Eric W. Kiernans, president of the Montreal and Canadian stock exchanges, said Thursday night it is time for Canada to shake off its unnatural conservatism and to apply for associate membership in the European common market.
Later on he says this:
Emotional exhortations about the traditional ties that bind the commonwealth countries will have little effect on the hard decisions that must be made by Great Britain and by ourselves.
In another article from the Gazette, entitled "Bankers for Most Canadian Businessmen" the following report appears:
G. Arnold Hart, A. T. Lambert and F. William Nicks-the presidents respectively of the Bank of Montreal, Toronto-Dominion Bank and Bank of Nova Scotia-not surprisingly, make much the same point in their addresses to annual meetings. They emphasize the urgency of being realistic about Britain's application for membership in the common market-Mr. Hart: "A positive approach... instead of merely opposing changes from existing arrangements;" Mr. Lambert: "... exploiting the opportunities ..." rather than "negative reaction of dismay"; Mr. Nicks: "...face realistically the changes that have taken place in Europe and seek ways of adapting ourselves to them."

These are typical of the reactions of business leaders from coast to coast. They are outward looking. They are forward looking. They know that Canada must take a positive initiative and not continue, as it has been doing, on a negative course. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) returned to Canada and found that people here were making statements along this line and that Canadian public opinion was not what he had expected while he was away, he accused the opposition of using the big lie tactics in referring to what he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said. I have in my hand a newspaper report headed: "Fleming Hits 'Big Lie' Use by Liberals". It reads in parts as follows:
Toronto-Finance Minister Fleming accused the Liberal party last night of using "big lie" tactics in attacking the government's position regarding Britain's possible entry to the European common market.
Mr. Fleming said there has been "distortion" of the position taken by Canada at the recent commonwealth economic conference at Accra, Ghana.
This is a serious charge, Mr. Speaker. Just to set the record straight I should like to read to you what the Minister of Finance had said just a few days previously in London. I have in my hand a press report headed, "Accra Statement 'Underplayed'-Fleming Raps Market Plans-With Greater Emphasis". It is by Duart Farquharson, of the Journal London bureau and it reads in part as follows:
The head-on clash between Britain and the overseas commonwealth countries at the Accra finance ministers meeting was not exaggerated but underplayed by the British press, according to Canadian Finance Minister Fleming.
To set the record straight, Mr. Fleming last week called in leading British correspondents covering the international monetary fund meeting in Vienna. With great emotion, he argued that commonwealth countries were unanimous in their condemnation of Britain's attempt to join the common market. They were not merely striking up bargaining postures, but sincerely believed that such a British move was bound to result in the disintegration of the commonwealth.
That is very strong language, Mr. Speaker, and it is in direct conflict with what the Minister of Finance said in Canada a few weeks later. It is necessary to check because the minister, when he accuses the opposition of using "big lie" tactics is just refuting the facts which he himself so carefully put on the record. It reminds us of his performances in this house on other occasions in the not too distant past. We are really shocked at his short memory.
Is a change coming in the government's position? Many people have thought so and there were some indications that this was so. But now it is obvious that the government has not really changed its attitude. This is reflected in reports based on the speech from the throne and subsequent interrogation in this

house. I wish to refer briefly to two press reports. One is from the Gazette of January 15:
The Canadian government, though reiterating support for freer world trade, hasn't committed itself to joining the proposed United States attempt to get major reductions in world tariff barriers.
That was made evident Saturday at the close of two days of informal trade talks between cabinet members of the two countries.
Then in an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of February 2, 1962, under the heading, "Negative Still?" we find the following:
Despite its protestations to the contrary, It seems apparent that the government still has no positive policy towards Britain's proposed entry into the European common market, and that it is not yet giving the vigorous leadership the situation demands.
This is most unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, and it is a matter of concern that the government is still negative in its position. It must change. It must adopt a more liberal attitude or Canada may be left as a tiny island isolated from the main stream of world events. The problem-encompassing some of the things about which I have spoken, such as interest rates, immigration, deficits and world trade

is to get Canada growing again. This is the problem which was not faced in the speech from the throne.
There is a growing awareness in Canada that our economy is falling short of its potential. The evidence is all around us, with high levels of unemployment despite the absence of a recession, and an actual decline of the order of 4 per cent since 1956 in the per capita production of goods and services. This evidence corroborates the increasing gap between what we produce and what we can produce. This chronic slack is at the root of our present economic difficulties. To draw attention to this gap is not to wallow in doom and gloom but to emphasize the extent to which we are currently failing to achieve our great potential.
No one can put a price tag on human dignity, humiliation, and frustration at not being able to earn a living. This is one of the incalculable costs. There are, however, two other costs involved which can be measured. First is the cost of carrying the unemployed. Some insight into the magnitude of this cost can be derived from the $900 million depletion of the unemployment insurance fund since December of 1956, and the $250 million spent as the federal share of unemployment assistance schemes financed jointly with the provinces. Much greater is the cost in terms of goods and services that could have been produced had we been able to reduce unemployment as a percentage
The Address-Mr. Keays of our labour force since 1957 to the postwar average, between January 1946 and June 1957, of 3.3 per cent. Since June, 1957, unemployment has averaged 6.2 per cent.
Nor do these levels of unemployment in themselves adequately measure the lack of growth in our economy. Much of the lack of growth is hidden in the short hours worked and in the failure to achieve the levels of productive efficiency that accompany operating at full capacity.
During the entire post-war period, 1946 to 1956, Canadians produced on the average 4.5 per cent more goods and services each year than in the previous year. If this trend had continued through 1961, we would have produced $5.2 billion more than last year. If this had occurred, Mr. Speaker, we would have a surplus now instead of a deficit. This would amount to $100 million a week more goods and services produced than we did in fact produce. No nation can take any satisfaction out of falling that far short of its proven capacity.
Even though the production has been lost, the potential remains. Canadian workers still possess the skills and the drive they exhibited during the post-war era. There has been no excessive depletion of our natural resources. The only resource we are wasting is time. The Canadian economy, since this government has come to power, has been marking time.

Mr. Speaker, as an introduction to my participation in this debate, may I be allowed to associate myself with those who have expressed warm words of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Bourdages) and seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Their contribution constituted a truly comprehensive review of the beneficial effects to our economy resulting from the actions taken by this government.
May I at the outset refer to a speech made in this debate by the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud), truly a great friend of mine. I should like however to endeavour to set the record straight as it relates to a few things he mentioned. He did refer to the fact that there were rumours the fishermen were being taken out of the unemployment insurance fund. There is definitely no reason for alarm, Mr. Speaker, but it is unfortunate that rumours such as this one do instil fear in the minds of these brave fishermen who, as every hon. member of this house knows, earn their living in a rather difficult way.

The Address-Mr. Keays
The unemployment insurance fund was established some 20 years ago at a time when conditions were vastly different from those existing today. The coverage of the fund has been extended, and as a result the complexities have been increased. However, this government is aware of the situation and, as in all other cases, has taken action by creating a commission of inquiry to study the effects of seasonal employees on the fund, and to decide upon some other method of taking care of the needs of these seasonal employees. All the members of this government who were in oppsition when the fund was established were aware of the complexities which would develop with the administration of the fund. They were also sure it would not be possible to continue operating the fund on a sound actuarial basis because, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) mentioned, humanitarian reasons compel certain actions. The results have been contrary to the arguments of the mathematicians.
It is also well to bear in mind that since 1957 fishermen have contributed about $5,554,000 to the fund in payments and have received benefits in the amount of $44,706,000. There are also other categories of seasonal workers, such as the inland water transport workers and the loggers. The contributions from logging and lumbering amounted to $4,046,592, and benefits paid amounted to $30,289,530. Although a study is now being made, I certainly would not wish the fishermen to believe there is any danger they are going to be excluded from the benefits of this fund. The study will probably result in the creation of a special fund for seasonal employees. Alternatively, a new fund might be created that would give an incentive to work and an interest on the part of these employees in setting up a savings fund to be matched by the government and the employer.
The hon. member for Kent also referred to the grants made to the province of Newfoundland, to the fishermen of Newfoundland. I do not believe the premier of New Brunswick took the same action as the premier of Newfoundland. Perhaps he is not concerned with the plight of the fishermen and did not ask for the co-operation and help of the federal government. I believe this answers the inquiry: the province of Newfoundland was concerned with the fishermen while New Brunswick and Quebec were not.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we should now look at the economic situation in our country. After all, the barometer of success or failure of an administration in this respect is our gross national product, which is the yardstick for measuring the total amount of goods and

services produced in a country. In order to look at this we must make a comparison, and I shall do so by comparing 1956 and 1961. Our gross national product in 1956 amounted to $30.6 billion and in 1961 to $37.4 billion. In other words, there was an increase of 22 per cent over 1956. With the last quarter of 1961 going at the rate of $39 billion, we can expect an increase in 1962 of 7 per cent or 8 per cent, bringing the gross national product of 1962 to $40.2 billion. As I have said previously, this is the barometer of success or failure and I believe that every hon. member of this house will admit such an increase would indicate the success of this administration. By any gauge surely we can all agree that this result has been phenomenal and that the economy is in high gear. Again, for the sake of comparison, let us return to 1956, although I hate to turn back for such proof.
In 1957 the government of the day had a surplus budget of $257.5 million. This large surplus was the result of post-war activities and was due to increases in exports to those nations devastated by the second world war and the Korean war. In Europe the industrial plants had disappeared. Facilities of production were completely wiped out and a whole rebuilding job had to be done. Much of that surplus was also brought about by filling orders for export, thus causing more employment at home and creating higher domestic purchasing power and consumer spending. However, although this was a nice budgetary surplus I often wonder why it was allowed to be wasted. By the norms of any good administration, part of the surplus could have been put to better use.
When we repair the roof of a house we repair it when the sun is shining, and it was in those days that action should have been taken by the government to prepare for the following years. Instead, the government was satisfied to sit back, become lazy and complacent. Was there no incentive to look ahead? Had the government done so at that time it would have seen the darkening clouds approaching, bringing in their path the evils of unemployment and suffering. Had the manifesto or economic program which we hear so much about today been brought out in 1956-but no one ever heard of such a thing in those days-possibly we would not have had to face the economic ills of 1957 and 1958.

During their prosperous years they did not impose overtaxation, draining revenues from their corporations and impeding progress. Trade within the community expanded by 45 per cent since the treaty of Rome went into operation, and their exports, taking all six together, increased over 50 per cent in the same year. What did the Conservative government do in 1957 when faced with this unpalatable situation? They went to work through the able Minister of Finance, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Labour, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture. Public works programs were immediately set in operation to alleviate the serious conditions of that time. The government increased the housing program until today we have reached the point where we are the largest builders per capita in the world in this field. It represents 18 per cent of our gross national product as against 11 per cent in the United States and 8 per cent in the United Kingdom.
The Department of Labour by extension .of the benefit periods, by aid to the provinces for vocational training, by a contribution to trade schools whereby competent people were trained to meet the changes caused by automation and advanced technology helped to bring about a situation in which production of commodities never before manufactured in Canada has been achieved.
The Department of Finance, by lowering the exchange rate on the Canadian dollar provided the main stimulus for an upturn in our economy and a consequent, eventual balanced budget. That department also helped
The Address-Mr. Clermont by providing greater loans to small businesses, and by extending the lending facilities of the industrial development bank and by guarantee loans to fishermen and farmers.
With the assistance of the Department of Trade and Commerce bold and imaginative measures were undertaken, such as the promotion of regional trade conferences which have now awakened Canadians to the possibilities of export. The department has also provided export facilities and has assisted in the creation of a productivity council, a body of proven administrators, the aim of which has been defined by its chairman, George DeYoung, as making industry more remunerative, more rewarding for the four groups affected by it-owners, employees, customers and the government. This council has also brought about a change in the thinking of some of the leaders of government, as indicated in the baby budget. It has also brought about a new thinking on the part of some of the industrial leaders in both primary and secondary industry, and there has been a change in the thinking of some of the senior leaders of labour who have been most helpful and co-operative in the establishment of this council.
What a tremendous amount of work has had to be done. Mr. Speaker, could you visualize the past administration willing to undertake that task? They would have given up the ghost long ago. It took a party with a true Canadian spirit and a national history of confidence and vigour, a party with fingertip feeling, faith and confidence, clearness of mind and decision of purpose. The task is not completed, and the results of past undertakings are the incentives to take Canadians to greater heights, to full employment and prosperity.

Transformers with the capacity to increase or to decrease voltage came into use, permitting current at high voltage to be transmitted at low cost and
The Address-Mr. Fournier then to be decreased in voltage at various points to serve the domestic or small consumers. Long distance lines were built with control stations at various centres with switching gear, regulation fusing and so on. While this early transformation was taking place, people became more and more conscious of electrical energy and its uses around the clock. It was then accepted as part of our economy and a great necessity. This summary covers the period extending from the 1900's up to the early 1920's and brings me to the second item, namely what was achieved.
While this development took place at a very high rate of speed, one problem was the production of electrical energy to meet the growing demand. In the early years of the nineties electricity was produced by small generators in the various communities, municipalities, villages and cities and in private industries. Fortunes were spent to provide mechanical devices, such as the diesel power of those days and thermal coal burning plants, steps were taken toward the harnessing of our rivers. This was all to the good, but as the demand increased so rapidly, by the early 1920's many of those limited resources were either exhausted or were beyond the financial ability of the owner.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. That is the time when, in practically every province across Canada, decisions were taken to pool all available resources in order to produce more and cheaper electrical energy to meet the demand, with the result that we saw in many provinces the birth of electric power commissions and the establishment of a provincial grid system. That was the result of a continuing growth in the demand for electric energy. Larger and more effective plants were built. The building of thermal coal burning plants at the mine site, the development of hydraulic power generators all connected together as one unit, saved millions of dollars to the citizens of the provinces and made large volumes of energy available. This is what has been done up to the present time and brings me to the third part of my remarks.
Today, in the early '60's, every province finds itself in about the same situation as that in which were all the communities in the early '20's, but on a larger scale. Today many provinces across the country have just about exhausted their resources for producing

The Address-Mr. Fournier electrical energy. We have reached a rate of growth which requires that the capacity must be doubled every seven and a half years, something which is just about impossible financially or otherwise in some provinces. If we review for the moment the position of the provinces and their resources for the production of electricity, we find Nova Scotia and New Brunswick with a limited coal field and limited hydraulic resources now in production of power. We find Quebec with the world's largest hydraulic potential and with less than 30 per cent of its potential developed. We find Ontario with natural resources just about exhausted, the prairie provinces with limited hydraulic resources but very rich in coal deposits and British Columbia with some hydraulic developments to meet today's situation.
Let us see what could be done for the future. The transmission of electric energy has become possible more economically by using direct current and converters. To energize a national grid, the maritime provinces have the world's largest tidal power potential. Better than 5 million kilowatts can be produced. Newfoundland, at one site alone on the Grand Falls river can produce another 5 million kilowatts. The capacity of this tremendous Grand Falls hydro plant would work well to balance the load during the dull period of tidal power. Today, Mr. Speaker, it is possible to use the tides to generate power 20 hours out of every 24. New types of generators have made it possible to produce power with the uptide as well as the downtide. At times, even hydro power plants have dull periods at low water and one cannot operate efficiently without assistance from another source. The building of the Chignecto canal would be the first step towards the development of maritime tidal power.
Then, we move to Quebec, with its vast hydraulic reserves. Ontario is turning to nuclear power, thanks to our generous government. This power, developed by nuclear energy, could be directed east or west through a national grid system. Then, we come to the immense coal and gas reserves of the prairies and at the extreme west we have the Columbia and Fraser rivers, those great potential sources of hydro energy which can be converted to electrical energy and carried across Canada to the points where it can be used to the advantage of the Canadian people.
This, Mr. Speaker, is just a brief review of the proposed grid system. Before we see this system in operation, hundreds of problems will have to be solved. The physical possibilities, the feasibility, administrative organization and countless other problems will need extensive study. This will require the labour, sweat and
IMr. Fournier.]
full co-operation of everyone involved. Let us not be alarmed by this irresponsible young Quebec minister of resources who has made a name for himself in other fields, but not in electricity. He is making himself a name, but the dignity of this house does not permit it to be mentioned.
Three years ago the then premier of New Brunswick, in co-operation with the good and generous federal government of today and the Hon. Robert Stanfield, premier of Nova Scotia, decided to build the first interprovincial grid system between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I was fortunate, as chairman of the New Brunswick electric power commission and in co-operation with the Nova Scotia power commission, in having a hand in the construction of this grid system. Today, power may be generated at Halifax or the extreme end of Nova Scotia, or at Edmundston in New Brunswick, and may be transported across these two provinces like lightning. A central distribution centre, with operating dispatchers having full control of generation and distribution, is located in the centre of the system. The savings in spare capacity alone to each province already represents several millions of dollars.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the good name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) will remain in history as the founder of this national grid system. Since it will be the greatest achievement of the sixties I am proud, along with my colleague and former boss the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming), to be associated with this great project. I hope that at the next election the people of Canada will realize the importance of this grid system to the future of our country and the future of our children. I hope, too, that the Canadian people are now convinced that the only responsible government able to accomplish the construction of this national grid system is the present Diefenbaker Conservative government. This government has proven beyond any doubt to the Canadian people it has ability in all spheres of administration. This government will not embark on such a large project without a full study of the feasibility of its operation. It always places the welfare of the citizens and the economy of the country first.
I was amused to hear some members of the opposition already questioning the merits of such a grid system. They asked, who is going to participate? How will it operate? They have already found fault with it. These electrical experts have already condemned the job before its birth. They want to know if it will be a boy or a girl. Will he be born with hair or will he be bald? What will be the colour of his or her eyes? These are but some

of the many ridiculous questions they ask. No one can answer questions as to how this grid system will be put together, who will take part in it or how it will work. These answers cannot be given until a lengthy and complete study is made in all the provinces, and that is exactly what this government intends to do. The government has proven this by inviting every province in the dominion to a meeting to set in operation the machinery for such a study. This organizational work is not completed overnight. In my opinion, what seems to disturb my friends most is the fact that the grid system, when completed, will not display a commemorative plaque reading, designed by Mike; engineered by Paul; supervised by Lionel and twisted by Jack. It is my hope that the opposition will show more horse sense in the future and stop finding fault with a project that does not even exist.
