speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour for me, and for the people of my riding of Trinity-Conception whom I have the privilege of representing, to join previous speakers in this traditional debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At this time, I should like to join my colleagues on both sides of the house in congratulating the mover, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and seconder, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) on their contribution to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am personally glad to see you, Mr. Speaker, again assuming the very important position which you have so capably and justly filled ever since you have occupied it.
I should like also to congratulate the Deputy Speaker upon his appointment to that very important post. I believe he will carry out efficiently the new duties entrusted to him. I am not forgetting the reappointment of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) as deputy chairman of committees of the whole house, who performed his duties in this important position during the last session of parliament to the complete satisfaction of all hon. members and with great credit to himself and to his riding. My congratulations also go to our former deputy speaker, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and to the parliamentary secretaries on their reappointment.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to talk about matters pertaining to the welfare of Canada's newest province. Since becoming the tenth province of Canada at the date of confederation, Newfoundland has progressed in many ways, especially in the
The Address-Mr. Tucker field of education, culminating in the expansion of Memorial university. During the year 1961, all was not sunny for the province and people of Newfoundland, but with the ups and downs the province did progress economically as well as educationally.
Newfoundland has suffered practically every summer from the curse of forest fires. Last year she saw her forests devastated by fires which were considered to be the worst in the history of the pulp and paper industry. Millions of dollars worth of woodlands were destroyed. The damage to the forests was so great that the prospects for a third paper mill in Newfoundland seemed in danger because of the loss of wood to supply the three paper mills. The latest news, which is good news, is that a third paper mill will very likely be established in Newfoundland. Although all the details have not been worked out, negotiations have been continuing for some time, and the prospects are bright.
This paper mill will be established, it is expected, near Come-By-Chance in the federal riding of Trinity-Conception. At the moment, the Bowater Pulp and Paper Company of Corner Brook has agreed with the premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Smallwood, to start logging operations this year in Labrador. Newfoundland now has two large paper mills, perhaps the largest in the world, one at Grand Falls and the other at Corner Brook. These mills employ hundreds of Newfoundlanders in steady employment. Indeed both the paper mills actually support modern towns which have sprung up and been laid out adjacent to each mill. With a third mill at Come-By-Chance, and with another large town to come into existence, Newfoundland's economy will receive a badly needed substantial boost.
During the forest fire period the provincial government of Newfoundland threw everything into fighting the fires, in an effort to save our valuable wood stands. It even went so far as to solicit and receive help from the federal government which lent troops, water planes and other fire fighting equipment. Newfoundland is singularly blessed with valuable wood stands and forests and the natural resources of these forests are of particular importance to Newfoundland. They play a large part in her economy. The forests provide the raw materials which keep her two large paper mills operating at full capacity the whole year round.
Her forests have been a great boon to the people of Newfoundland in setting up her economy and leading to the building of two large and beautiful cities. It now appears that Newfoundland is about to get a third paper mill and her forests will also provide the raw

The Address-Mr. Tucker materials for it. In that section of the province her people can look forward to another new town coming into existence in the near future, with employment being available to the people in the area. All in all the forests of Newfoundland play an important part in the economy of our province and will continue to do so, perhaps on a larger scale in the future than in the past. Consequently the menace of forest fires must be controlled and, if at all possible, entirely eliminated.
Perhaps the greatest advance made by Newfoundland since the date of confederation has been in the field of education. The provincial government has gone all out with its financial and other assistance to education and the building of new schools, new regional high schools, and as a crowning success we have the Memorial University of Newfoundland, so that our present government has often been termed "the government of schools". Since confederation more new schools have been built, opened and staffed than in the time between the discovery of Newfoundland and the date of confederation, which shows that Newfoundland is really on the march in the field of education. Newfoundland's university recently opened its new buildings with pageantry and pomp and it will soon be one of the greatest universities in Canada. At the present time some of the halls of learning to make up the entire university are only in the planning stages. When the university is completed it will be second to none in Canada and will be a worthy memorial to Newfoundland's gallant dead in both world wars.
The fisheries industry will always be an important industry to Newfoundland, contrary to the present day thinking of some politicians. Newfoundland was a fishing country even before its official discovery and down through the years she has charted the measure of her success or failure by her yearly catch. A poor fishery meant a poor year for Newfoundland and her people. A good fishery meant a prosperous year for Newfoundland. However, since Newfoundland became a province of Canada she has not advanced her fisheries in the new techniques and methods of catching and curing fish, such as are used by Russia, Iceland, and other foreign nations fishing on our doorsteps.
The past year has been one of the poorest fishery years in the history of Newfoundland, coupled with several storms which caused damage and destruction to both public and private property, to the tune of approximately $250,000 in one single storm, leaving many of our fishermen almost destitute. Time and time again the federal government of Canada has been urged to see that a thorough investigation be made into our fisheries, that measures

should be taken and support given to bringing our fisheries up to date in both catching and curing methods. It was also urged that Canada should have already taken some action toward establishing the 12 mile limit to protect our Canadian fishermen and fisheries.
On many occasions Newfoundland fishermen claimed that foreign vessels were fishing inside the three mile zone, and several times they have stated that their fishing gear was damaged by foreign ships. Last spring a Newfoundland sealing captain gave me a flag of a foreign ship which he stated was definitely picked up inside the three mile limit when the ship was operating inside that limit.
The banks of Newfoundland are becoming more and more crowded every year with foreign fishing ships and the time has long passed when we should have begun protecting our fishing grounds. The present Canadian government fears that we would offend some of our friendly foreign countries if we were to establish a 12 mile limit for territorial waters and put real teeth into the provisions to enforce it.
Two years ago the government of Iceland became concerned over its fishermen's livelihood and unilaterally extended her traditional three mile limit to 12 miles. This was vigorously opposed by Great Britain, an old friend of Iceland, but on occasion Icelandic patrol vessels interfered with British draggers. On one occasion a British man-of-war went along as escort to British fishing vessels, and incidentally I have heard that man-of-war was captained by a Newfoundlander. Iceland's 12 mile limit is now recognized by Britain, with a three year phase out, during which British vessels may be allowed to fish in certain areas up to six miles from amended base lines.
Today Newfoundland finds that in and around her shores, where her waters at one time were teeming with fish, there are more Russians and other foreign nationals fishing than there are Newfoundlanders. The seal fishery, once a prosperous venture for Newfoundlanders, has been practically taken over by Norway and the wealth taken from our very shores. However, there does not seem to be anything done about it, or any assistance forthcoming from the federal government of Canada to investigate new methods and procedures for the seal fishery, in order that the wealth which is now benefiting the economy of other countries could be kept in Canada, and particularly in Newfoundland. In my opinion the time has arrived when we must give consideration to seal conservation by placing a closed season on the killing of seals off the east coast of Newfoundland.
Newfoundland badly needs federal and provincial government assistance for her fisheries, if they are to survive and be one

of the chief industries of our province; because it is plain to see that Newfoundland fisheries are very important to that province and are still one of the major components that make up her economy. For the success of her fisheries Newfoundland urgently needs more public cold storage for both bait and fish. Without such storage facilities her fisheries cannot expand or enlarge. More community stages are also required. The fisheries are a big cog in the wheel of her economy and they must be protected and developed, as the economy of Canada as a whole requires and needs them.
Mr. Speaker, not so many years ago most of the people of Newfoundland were isolated because of very poor roads, and often because there were no roads at all. The picture has changed vastly, and because of the trans-Canada highway and the many local roads which have been built in the past 13 years isolation is practically unknown on the island. Again, when one considers that the cost of building and maintaining roads in Newfoundland is higher than in any other province of Canada, one realizes what a tremendous job of shedding isolation has been accomplished by those concerned with this program.
Since Newfoundland still has to contend with her narrow gauge railway, after being a province of Canada for 13 years, we consider that as a matter of equity the federal government should complete the unfinished portion or portions of Newfoundland's trans-Canada highway to compensate for her railway not being the standard gauge of the other provinces of Canada. We have not forgotten the promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in 1957 to give us a standard gauge railway.
Newfoundland still needs more and better roads, more connecting roads, and above all she really needs the completion of her section of the trans-Canada highway. This completion of the trans-Canada highway will be delayed for years, and with it the economy of Newfoundland checkmated, unless the federal government soon realizes Newfoundland's position in the matter, recognizes her rightful claim to a standard gauge railway and makes a compromise or gives further financial assistance. Because the trans-Canada highway is not completed Newfoundland and her economy will suffer in regard to the tourist business. The tourist business in Newfoundland, goes a long way toward supporting our economy, and it could do much more. This industry is really considered too important a revenue item to be lost.
Since the days of confederation Newfoundland has rightly come into her own in the 26207-1-72
The Address-Mr. Tucker mining field. Already iron ore, copper, zinc, talc and gold in small quantities have been discovered and mined; but the latest development at Carol lake, being developed by the Labrador Mining Company-this is a new discovery-has placed Newfoundland in the forefront of the iron ore market and she is now Canada's largest producer of this commodity. Last year our mineral production was worth $96 million. Bell island, the iron ore island of Newfoundland, has been our main industry on the island for many years. The ore from Bell island has been steadily and continuously going into the markets of the world and has always been in fair demand. During the past five or six years the picture for Bell island has been continuously changing due to world conditions. The past two years have seen Bell island feel the pinch because of short orders for her ore, with the consequent loss of employment for many Bell island and Conception bay miners. Surveys for 1962 are not too bright and it is anticipated that unless world conditions change and further orders are received for ore, Bell island mines will close down for at least an indefinite period. At the present time the picture is far from encouraging.
In recent years mining has become very important in the financial and economical structure of Newfoundland because it appears that Newfoundland is now only on the thresh-hold of great developments in mining. At present only the surface has been scratched. Some of the biggest financial companies and combines of companies have acquired mining rights in Newfoundland and it is confidently anticipated that in the foreseeable future mining activities in Newfoundland will reach proportions that will make this industry the highlight of the century.
Mr. Speaker, compared with a quarter of a century ago, the budgeted expenditures for one year to cover the services of all departments in Newfoundland are now equalled by the expenditures of two departments, health and welfare. The medical and social services inaugurated in Newfoundland since confederation could not be contemplated 20 or 25 years ago, and the only drawback to further rapid expansion is the lack of doctors and nurses.
The advances made in hospital accommodation and medical and social services since the advent of confederation have been phenomenal, but the need is still not satisfied because Newfoundlanders need more hospital accommodation, doctors and trained nurses. However, Newfoundland can be justly proud
1120	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Tucker of her program of hospital and medical services because she has the highest birth rate and the lowest death rate of all the provinces of Canada.
I should now like to discuss one of our greatest problems, that of unemployment. Because Newfoundland is an island, one of her principal sources of revenue to sustain her economy is her fishery. This is the principal occupation of her residents. If the fishery is good in one year, then the employment problem in that year is not so great; but in a year of poor fishery or failure in the fishery the employment problem becomes acute. Seasonal employment in Newfoundland cannot be avoided, because the principal industries or labour offering enterprises, the fishery, logging, seal fishery, road building and construction work, are all seasonal employment. Consequently during the offseasons in these industries Newfoundland will have a great deal of unemployment because there is nothing to offer to the people to temporarily take up the slack.
Another factor which one must consider when studying this problem of seasonal unemployment in Newfoundland is the large percentage of her labour force which comes under the category of unskilled workmen. This is the class of workers who cannot afford to be unemployed. Thus we are faced with this difficulty each year.
Let us first look for at least a partial remedy for this problem. I consider that getting more people back into the fishing industry is very important, even if the federal and provincial governments have to provide extra assistance, especially during the coming fishery season, because due to storms, losses, and the like, many fishermen will not have the equipment with which to engage in the fishery this year without financial help. As to a long term cure, it will be necessary for our fisheries in Newfoundland to be placed on a sound footing and brought up to date in methods and procedures. Our fishermen should have all the mechanical devices that are used by the Russians, in order to make fishing a success. The government of Canada owes this to her fishermen.
Much remains to be done on the marketing side. Canadians do not eat enough fish. More marketing research must be conducted under federal auspices. A national fish marketing board could go a long way toward inducing Canadians to eat more fish.
The erection of a third paper mill and the creation of a new town of Labrador and perhaps one at Come-By-Chance, where it is hoped a mill will be erected, will tend to reduce unemployment. But what is really


needed more than anything else is the creating and setting up of factories or industries in larger towns such as Lewisporte, Harbour Grace, Carbonear, Clarenville, Catalina, Port Union, St. John's, Corner Brook and Grand Falls, where many workers, particularly young workers could be gainfully employed in their home towns. It may well be that young people cannot always afford to accept opportunities offered to them elsewhere because they have to care for aged or sickly parents, or undertake similar responsibilities. If the suggestion I have made were followed it would lead to a reduction in unemployment, and I urge the government to give the idea their immediate attention and consideration.
I have outlined the serious problems that still face Newfoundland. Again I say that we need the help of the Canadian government as a team if we are to reach our goal of complete employment by creating jobs at home, thus making Newfoundland a more stable element in this country's economic structure.
Newfoundland's first oil refinery, operated by the Golden Eagle Company of Canada at Conception Bay, went on stream early in December 1961. It is a $7,500,000 plant and it will produce approximately 8,500 barrels daily, employing about 100 permanent employees. About 25 per cent of the plant's production will be shipped out of the province, and the provincial government will provide the refinery's initial market. Fuels, lubricating oils and asphalt will be produced for distribution in eastern Canada. Marine terminals have been built in Corner Brook, Botwood, Clarenville, Montreal and Rimouski. The company expects that the value of its assets will increase in value in 10 years from $15 million, as at present, to $75 million.
In closing I should like to say that I was glad to learn from the speech from the throne that Her Majesty the Queen Mother together with Their Highnesses, the Duke of Edinburgh and the Princess Royal will visit Canada some time during the coming summer. I sincerely hope their visit will be a happy one.

speechtext:
It is
with pleasure that I rise to take part in this throne speech debate. In accordance with the time honoured custom my first words will be those of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the address, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) upon his elevation to the position of Deputy Speaker. At this time I also wish to extend congratulations to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his appointment to the position of Minister of Mines and

Technical Surveys. We look forward to seeing this minister more often in Nova Scotia as his department extends its new hydrographic and oceanographic base at Halifax.
The speech from the throne represents a monumental work on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his cabinet. Opposition speakers to date have made it their business to steer away from this blueprint of further national development. However, I believe this government has charted a course, has laid down a program, which will provide a higher standard of living and greater opportunity within a free economy for all Canadians.
It is not possible, in the short time available, for me to deal with all the progressive plans enunciated in the speech from the throne, so I shall limit myself to dealing with a few matters of significance and importance to our area. There are representatives here from all parts of Canada who are quite capable of outlining conditions as they exist in their localities, and I therefore propose to confine my remarks for the most part to Nova Scotia and to the developments taking place in that province.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he spoke in the debate, I am sorry he is not in his place today.
It appeared to me he must still believe he is on the sunny beaches of Acapulco, far removed from the pulse of the Canadian economy and the Canadian people. He kept calling for an election, saying the Liberals have the answer. When the election comes, he added, it would be on the record of this government. We on this side of the house will certainly welcome and accept that challenge. I remember well the election of 1957. It was fought on the record of the then Liberal government in office-and the Leader of the Opposition knows the result. The election of 1958 was fought on the record of the Conservative government in office, and the results of that election are painfully evident to the hon. gentleman as he looks over at the benches occupied by government supporters and then to the tattered remnants of his once great party. It was in these campaigns that the people of Nova Scotia looked to the present Prime Minister and, with a sailor's salute, said: Long may your big jib draw. Then they proceeded to elect 12 members from 12 constituencies in support of the Conservative party. These are times when the Leader of the Opposition must ask himself: What did we do wrong? At the time of their defeat it was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), I believe, who said they had neglected their clothes on the left bank while 26207-1-72i
The Address-Mr. Crouse in swimming and the Conservatives had slipped in from the right. The Leader of the Opposition had another viewpoint. In his opinion "the brass lost touch with the grass". However, today the hon. gentleman is critical of our Prime Minister and of members of this government for keeping in close touch with the people. I think it is time we enlightened the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) and pointed out that it was arrogance and indifference to the needs of the people that cost the Liberal party majority support in the Atlantic provinces. And this arrogance and indifference is still evident today, due no doubt to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition has the same old economic advisor he had in 1956. We heard the other day that Mr. Walter Gordon had been nominated to contest the Toronto Davenport riding in the next federal election. He is the man with bold imaginative policies-the man who has all the answers for the Liberals. Weil, let us look at some of the bold imaginative policies of maritime Gordon, this aspiring Liberal finance minister, as enunciated in the 1956 preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. I quote from page 98:
About one and three quarter million Canadians, or over 10 per cent of the total population, live in the Atlantic region. It is well known that the rate of economic progress in the three maritime provinces-Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island-was relatively slow for a long period of years.
The report continues:
It is a fact that average incomes in this region continue to lag behind the averages for the rest of Canada. In 1926, for example, the average income per capita in the three maritime provinces was 38 per cent below the average for the other six provinces: in 1939 the corresponding percentage was 32 per cent; in 1946 it was 24 per cent; and in 1955, 33 per cent. In 1955, the average income for the Atlantic provinces, including Newfoundland, was 37 per cent below the average for the other six provinces.
Then he continues:
The fact remains that living standards are lower in the Atlantic provinces than they are in the rest of Canada, and that it is in everyone's interest to reduce this differential if it is at all possible-
I repeat: "if it is at all possible"-
-to do so. It is not suggested that this should be accomplished by ad hoc projects and handouts. Such measures are as unpalatable to the recipients as they are to those who must foot the bills. What is required is a positive and comprehensive approach to the problems of the Atlantic region. With this as the objective, it is suggested that the people of Canada as a whole might be willing to assist the people of the Atlantic provinces in discovering, developing and making the best use of resources in that area.
If it should turn out that there is not the necessary combination of resources in sufficient quantities to permit a substantial rise in living standards in the Atlantic region, generous assistance

The Address-Mr. Crouse should be given to those people who might wish to move to other parts of Canada where there may be greater opportunities.

speechtext:
It continues:
But even if assistance is provided for those people who might be willing to move elsewhere, many people undoubtedly would prefer to remain where they are, despite the handicaps referred to. People who so choose should at the same time be prepared to accept a different kind of life, or certainly life at a different tempo, and lower levels of income.
Is this bold and imaginative? No Atlantic provinces grants here. This would be ad hoc assistance. I continue:
It would be unwise to spend large sums on the construction of highways merely for the purpose of forcing a reduction in railway rates by the introduction of highway truck competition and thus increasing the present losses of the railways. It would be equally unwise to insist upon the continuance of unprofitable rail services if, with the construction of road facilities, the present traffic could be handled effectively by trucks and buses.
Do away with the railways, build no roads or highways. That is what is recommended by Mr. Gordon and his party. If you read the whole report it can be summed up as only a negative, do-nothing, move-out policy.
But, the Liberals say, Mr. Gordon has changed. He is now the national chairman of the Liberal campaign, committee and his heart literally bleeds for the maritime provinces. I have in my hand a report of his speech delivered at Sutherlands River on December 14, 1961, as reported by the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. While we have heard of the new Pearson and the new Gordon they still have the same old policies for the Atlantic provinces and the evacuation of those provinces. Listen to these quotations from Mr. Gordon's speech:
Living standards In the Atlantic provinces were lower than in the rest of Canada, he said, and it was in everyone's interest to reduce the differential.
He stated that it was not suggested that this should be accomplished by "ad hoc" projects and handouts-such measures were as unpalatable to the recipients as to those who must foot the bill.
What was required, he said, was a positive and comprehensive approach to the problems of the Atlantic region.
And again:
There would be no point in anyone moving to Upper Canada, for example, in search of work these days.
And further:
Special measures will be needed for looking after these people and for re-establishing in other industries those who may be interested in such an alternative. It may be such measures could be included under the broad national scheme we have referred to for relocating people who may wish to abandon sub-marginal farms and be re-established in other industries.
In other words, the one suggestion Mr. Gordon did have for the citizens of the

Atlantic provinces has now been modified and he cannot even suggest a suitable province to which we should move. Mr. Speaker, we will stay in the Atlantic provinces. We do not need to move out. Under the progressive policies of the present federal government employment opportunities are gradually being provided for our people. We did not listen to Mr. Gordon in 1956 and apply to the then Liberal government for a one way ticket out of our province. Some of the figures I intend to place on the record will indicate what has happened to the good ship Nova Scotia since we discharged the entire mutinous crew of Liberals and the present Prime Minister became captain.
The average income per capita in the Atlantic provinces, as quoted by Mr. Gordon has always been lower than the average income in the other six provinces. However, we are making progress for, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, the average per capita personal income for the four Atlantic provinces increased from a low of $851 in 1956 to $1,010 in 1960. In the three maritime provinces, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the average income in 1960 was 32.8 per cent below the national average. We are still not out of the woods economically and the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants are still justifiable, but we have been making a far better showing in the last four years under this Conservative government than we made in the last 22 years under the Liberal government.
The transition in Nova Scotia that brought about this increase in income is apparent in the fishing industry, the boat and shipbuilding industry, the mining industry, agriculture and in the construction industry.

My hon. friends opposite do not like to hear these facts. I hear a comment from my hon. friend, the economist from Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). Nevertheless we are glad to state the facts even if my hon. friends do not like to hear them.
The Nova Scotia fishing industry is in the midst of an accelerated boat building and fish plant expansion program. This has been brought about by the far sighted, progressive legislation introduced by this government to assist the shipbuilding industry in Canada and the fishermen in particular. Already a number of new draggers in the 100 foot class have been launched, with more to follow before the end of 1962, and if you could but visit the wooden shipbuilding yards in Mahone Bay, Lunenburg, Dayspring and in

fact, most of the yards throughout Nova Scotia, you would see a scene reminiscent of former years when our province became famous as the home of wooden ships and iron men, and the schooner Bluenose sailed the north Atlantic undefeated. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald on February 8 headlined their front page with the statement that this shipbuilding boom could amount to $10 million this year. These new fishing draggers for the ground fish and scallop fishing industry will provide a safer working unit for the fishermen who will be stepping out of smaller boats, into modern efficient ships that will help ensure a year round supply of fish for the processing plants. And speaking of processing plants, Lunenburg Sea Products Ltd. is planning an $8 million expansion to their facilities at Lunenburg. The plant will be erected on an eight acre site, will provide additional jobs for 200 to 300 people, will add at least $4 million annually to the economy of Nova Scotia and is expected to be in production early in 1964. In addition to this, two new fish plants are under construction for Cape Breton island.
While all of us welcome this expansion and realize the value of the fishing industry, not only to Nova Scotia but to Canada as a whole, we are also aware of the growing need for well trained crews for the expanding fishing fleet. A modern fishing dragger is a highly complex unit containing many electronic devices to assist in locating good fishing grounds, as well as protect the crew in foggy weather. New fishing techniques should be introduced and I would suggest the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Transport give consideration to the establishment of special vocational training facilities for deep sea fishing vessel crews. Due to their environment and long hours of work, fishermen cannot always secure the technical training required. I hope the government will find it possible to initiate this type of training program in the near future.
In our mining industry there were major advances during the past year. Salt production increased 40 per cent, milling started at the Walton silver-lead-zinc ore body and initial steps were taken toward establishing a major new gypsum producer in Cape Breton. In fact, present resources of gypsum in Nova Scotia are sufficient to produce 2 million tons per year for the next hundred years, and this will contribute substantially to the economy of the province.
Interest in Nova Scotia as a leading source of industrial minerals continues to grow. The tempo of exploration last year was at an all time high and this bodes well for the future of our mining industry.
The Address-Mr. Crouse
In the field of agriculture in Nova Scotia, last year's records reached new heights. The gross income from farm products last year exceeded $53 million. Livestock and livestock products account for about 80 per cent of this amount which is an increase of more than $3 million over the previous year.
There was a time when if someone mentioned the Annapolis valley we thought only of apples. However, while apples remain one of the province's best known farm products, we see tobacco grown today commercially for the first time in our history. Last year's crop was estimated at $50,000 and present plans call for a crop of at least four times this size in 1962.
In the construction field and in the establishment of new industries the record is beyond compare. In my constituency the American boat building corporation has located at Mahone Bay. Yesterday's newspaper carried the report that they recently increased their working staff by 40 per cent. The Atlantic Bridge Company Limited at Lunenburg and the Lunenburg Foundry and Engineering Limited at Lunenburg recently built large new additions to their plants. Scotia Marine Products Limited at Lower Woods Harbour have established a $750,000 plant for the production of "algin", an end product of rock-weed which has almost unlimited possibilities as an emulsifying agent in ice cream and food supplements. This type of factory is quite rare, as there are only 10 other algin plants known to be in existence throughout the world. Other plants established have been the Bonda Meal and Oil Limited at Short Beach, Yarmouth county; Cossor Electronics Limited at Dartmouth; Fairey Aviation Company of Canada Limited at Halifax; Eastern Paper Box Manufacturing Limited at Halifax; Federal Products Limited at Truro; the $3 million Formex Company of Canada plant at Kentville; the Oxford Desk Limited at Oxford; Phillips Electrical Company at Dartmouth; Springhill Homes and Supplies, Springhill and the Sur-rette Battery Company in the same town; the $14 million Texaco oil refinery going up at Woodside in Dartmouth, the fourth big refinery in the Atlantic region with a 13,500 barrel capacity; Weymouth Industries Limited; and I could go on until I listed a total of 22 new industries in Nova Scotia in the past four years. While all this has been going on our existing industries have been growing and expanding and for the most part have been providing new jobs. All this has happened in a province where the only suggestions the Liberals had when they were in office, for the improvement of our lot was Mr. Gordon's classic, "move out".
Despite this record of progress and steady growth, under a Conservative government,

The Address-Mr. Crouse the hon. member tor Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud), asks what there is in the speech from the throne for the Atlantic provinces? He then proceeds to degrade the maritime area with a speech filled with doom and gloom that could only be exceeded by his leader. There are many items in the speech from the throne that will be of benefit to our area. For example, the extension of the winter works program, co-operative measures between the 10 provinces to encourage wise management of our natural resources; the provision of low cost electric power; the maintenance of fair prices for our farms and fisheries products; legislation extending farm and fisheries improvement loans acts; increases in welfare pensions to all classes; increases in civilian war pensions and allowances; increases to our university grants; institution of a second ferry service between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
These are but a few of the measures that will benefit our citizens in the Atlantic provinces. In my opinion the remarks made by the hon. member for Gloucester do great harm to our area by destroying the confidence of the investment world in locating industry in the Atlantic provinces. In support of this statement I quote from a recent editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald in which Mr. Karl A. Klausen, president of Nova Scotia Pulp Limited, stated Nova Scotia's excess of bad publicity has hampered its economic growth. I quote from the editorial as follows:
Mr. Klausen said he had been advised by pulp executives and foresters across Canada against establishing a mill in Nova Scotia and that financiers in Toronto and Montreal warned against the move because of lack of confidence in our economic future.
So far as this attitude begins at home, habits of thought and continual crying of havoc and hard times will have to give way to more reasoned appraisals of our strengths and weaknesses. For it is apparent that despite such soft spots as the coal industry the over-all economy of Nova Scotia, particularly in the vital field of manufacturing, is making some rapid strides-
As the President of Nova Scotia Pulp Limited stated, this province has a vast industrial potential and a prosperous economic future if we can persuade ourselves and others to believe in it.
The record proves that under this federal Progressive Conservative government we are growing stronger economically. I would suggest that we be non-partisan enough to give credit where credit is due so that new industries will locate with confidence in the Atlantic provinces and help to expand our employment opportunities.
The hon. member for Gloucester condemns this government for its lack of consideration of the problems facing these people of the Atlantic provinces. I ask him whether he is not aware of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants which provided $100 million

in the last four years to the Atlantic provinces and which will be increased to $175 million in the next five years with an additional grant of $8 million per annum to Newfoundland, in order to bolster our economy and to provide services to our people, which they could not otherwise afford owing to the disparity in our income. In his report Mr. Gordon went from 1926 to 1956, and with the exception of the five year period 1930 to 1935, this country was under the rule of a Liberal government. During those years the disparity in our income in the Atlantic provinces was as high as 38 per cent in relation to those in the rest of Canada. However, I cannot recall any member of the Liberal party advocating adjustment grants during those years and they are against them today; because Mr. Gordon has recently stated that he does not approve of ad hoc projects and handouts.
Another point worth mentioning is that these Atlantic provinces adjustment grants have no strings attached. They can be distributed at the discretion and pleasure of the four Atlantic premiers and there is no pressure brought to bear by this federal government as to how they will spend this money. As a result, we see today in the four Atlantic provinces, the greatest road building, school construction, and industrial assistance programs in our history, and our present population in Nova Scotia of 727,000 gradually increasing.
While I welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that a new ferry will be built to serve between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland I would also urge upon the government that further consideration be given to establishing a second ferry between Nova Scotia and Gloucester, Massachusetts. At the present time discussions are under way between Premier Stanfield and Governor John Volpe of Massachusetts, and a meeting was held in Boston on February 19, to discuss various proposals on this matter. In the opinion of many Nova Scotians, a second ferry service is required to supplement the one now provided by the M. V. Bluenose between Yarmouth and Bar Harbour, in order to increase our tourist industry which last year brought over $50 million in additional revenue from over 600,000 visitors. Nova Scotia is truly Canada's ocean playground with 5,000 miles of rugged shoreline, scores of sandy beaches, thousands of lakes and streams and a temperate climate. The present proposal is to have a second ferry operate from Gloucester, Massachusetts, to a port along the south shore, a trip of 10 to 12 hours, depending on the port chosen. When we realize that 33,800,000 people live within

a day's travel of Gloucester which is only 32 miles from Boston and 250 miles from New York, we get some idea of the tremendous tourist potential from this area. As Nova Scotia's fishing industry is expanding, and we ship over 75 per cent of our catch to the United States market, this additional ferry would also provide an improved service to this vitally important Nova Scotia industry. I hope the minister of trade and industry and the Minister of Transport will give careful consideration to this proposal so that steps may be taken to provide this additional service and improve still further the economic development of Nova Scotia which has made great forward strides under the present Conservative government.
